name: Mesterolone

lead: Mesterolone, best known as Proviron, is an oral androgen derived from dihydrotestosterone. Users add it to testosterone for libido, a drier and harder look, and, among younger users, as a way to raise DHT, sometimes under the label of puberty maxxing.

It is a 1-alpha-methyl derivative of DHT that acts on the androgen receptor and is not converted to estrogen. Clinically it has been used for male hypogonadism and tested for male infertility with mixed results. One detailed forum self-report described stronger erections and a slightly drier look with no change in strength or muscle mass; no study has examined its appearance effects.

paras: Users take it as an oral tablet, most often as an add-on to testosterone or other compounds rather than alone. Reported changes are mild and described over weeks of use.

One reference describes a low risk of liver toxicity relative to other oral androgens, but safety data in healthy users are limited to forum reports. Users raise DHT-related concerns such as hair loss and discuss whether use suppresses the natural hormonal axis. It is prohibited in sport.

angle.text: Mesterolone (Proviron) is a mild oral DHT derivative that users add for a harder, drier, more masculine look, libido and, among younger users, puberty-maxxing. It is used medically for hypogonadism and fertility; hair loss is a common concern among users.

lead: Mesterolone, sold mainly as Proviron, is an oral androgen: a synthetic version of dihydrotestosterone (DHT) with an added methyl group at the 1-alpha position, made by Schering and used in medicine for low testosterone and, more contentiously, for male infertility.[1][2] In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding circles it is used as an add-on to testosterone or other compounds, where users say it supports libido, a drier and harder look, and, in the puberty-maxxing discussion among younger users, a higher DHT effect.[3][4][5]

Pharmacologically it is a strongly androgenic but weakly anabolic compound. Wikipedia notes that skeletal muscle inactivates it through the enzyme 3-alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, that it is already 5-alpha-reduced so 5-alpha-reductase does not amplify it in skin, hair follicles or prostate, and that it is not converted to estrogen.[1] It binds sex-hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) unusually strongly, which proponents cite as the basis for the idea that it raises free testosterone.[1][6][2]

Published research is clinical and from the 1970s to 1990s: randomized fertility trials with mixed results, a double-blind comparison with testosterone undecanoate in hypogonadal men, a study in normal men and small mood studies.[7][8][9][10][11][12] None measured muscle, facial or skin appearance. Forum evidence consists of user reports, including one detailed solo trial that described stronger erections and a slightly drier look with no change in strength or size.[3]
infobox: 1966 (Neumann et al.); introduced by Schering c. 1967 [1]
Prescription drug in many countries; US Schedule III; not marketed in the US [1]

paras: Mesterolone is used clinically as androgen replacement in men with low testosterone and has been tested for idiopathic male infertility. Wikipedia also lists anemia and delayed puberty among reported uses, and notes it is rarely chosen for replacement today because testosterone preparations are standard.[1] In the appearance communities it is used as a supporting compound rather than a main one.

A double-blind randomized comparison of testosterone undecanoate and mesterolone in 26 hypogonadal men assessed effects on sexual activity and mental state.[10] Reviews of hypogonadism therapy discuss alternatives to testosterone, and studies of androgen substitution regimens examined effects on erythropoiesis, lipids, bone and prostate.[13][14][15][16][17] A trial in normal men examined mesterolone's effect on pituitary-testicular function.[11] Wikipedia notes that because mesterolone is not aromatized it has been considered for patients with breast tenderness or gynecomastia.[1]

For infertility, a 1987 randomized trial gave mesterolone or placebo to 40 men with idiopathic oligospermia for more than four months and found significant increases in semen volume, mean sperm concentration and total sperm count, with motility and morphology unchanged.[7] A 1983 randomized comparison of placebo, clomiphene, mesterolone, pentoxifylline and testosterone enanthate rebound therapy in 46 men found that placebo, mesterolone, pentoxifylline and rebound therapy did not significantly increase sperm concentration or partner pregnancy.[8] A placebo-controlled trial of high-dose mesterolone in idiopathic infertility was published in 1991, and a 1995 review lists mesterolone among weakly androgenic agents that had yielded little effect in male-factor infertility.[9][18] Reviews describe pharmacological infertility treatment as largely empirical, and a Cochrane review of androgens for idiopathic oligo/asthenospermia was later withdrawn.[19][20][21]

Looksmaxxing users describe mesterolone as an add-on to testosterone for libido and as a way to raise DHT. Threads ask whether it is useful at 15 or 17, whether it affects height or hair, whether it suppresses the hormonal axis, and whether an injectable form is sensible.[22][23][24][25][26] One post calls it the most underrated and safest compound for puberty-maxxing, while another titled a documented trial of Proviron alone as showing it is mostly cope.[4][3] No controlled study has examined these cosmetic claims.

Mesterolone is 1-alpha-methyl-DHT. It is an androgen receptor agonist with strong androgenic and weak anabolic activity.[1] Wikipedia explains the weak anabolic effect by skeletal muscle inactivating the molecule through 3-alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, which testosterone does not undergo, and says it has no estrogenic or progestogenic activity because it is not aromatized.[1] Because it is already 5-alpha-reduced, a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor such as finasteride would not be expected to block it, a point forum users raise in hair-loss threads.[1][27]

Mesterolone binds SHBG with high affinity; one study cited by Wikipedia put its affinity at about 440 percent of DHT's and another at 82 percent. The article says this may raise free testosterone by displacing it from SHBG.[1] A 1984 relative-binding study of anabolic steroids examined androgen-receptor binding in muscle and prostate alongside SHBG binding.[6] Grokipedia states that the free-testosterone idea lacks large clinical trials.[2]

The 1-alpha methyl group slows hepatic metabolism and makes the compound orally active, although Wikipedia gives an oral bioavailability of about 3 percent, protein binding of about 98 percent (about 40 percent albumin and 58 percent SHBG) and an elimination half-life of 12 to 13 hours.[1] Because it is not 17-alpha-alkylated, it is described as carrying little liver-toxicity risk, while its cardiovascular risk is described as comparable to other oral androgens.[1] Urinary metabolites, including long-term markers and markers in the sulfate fraction, have been characterised by mass spectrometry for doping control.[28][29]

Mesterolone has the formula C20H32O2 and a molar mass of about 304.5 g/mol; it is a synthetic androstane steroid. Wikipedia lists related compounds as metenolone and its esters, the antiandrogen rosterolone, and the 17-alpha-methylated analogue Demalon.[1]

Mesterolone was described by 1966 by Neumann and colleagues and introduced for medical use by Schering by about 1967 under the Proviron brand.[1] Schering had earlier used the Proviron name, from 1936, for testosterone propionate, which was afterwards sold as Testoviron.[1] A 1973 clinical report examined it in male infertility and a 1974 controlled study measured pituitary-testicular function in normal men.[30][11]

The infertility trials ran from the 1980s to the early 1990s with mixed outcomes, and the Cochrane review that pooled androgen trials for idiopathic oligo/asthenospermia was withdrawn in 2007.[7][8][9][21] Its adoption in bodybuilding and, later, looksmaxxing forums as an adjunct came decades afterwards; Wikipedia notes it is not commonly used by athletes for muscle because of its weak anabolic activity.[1]

Clinical studies include randomized trials in idiopathic oligospermia (a 1987 placebo-controlled trial in 40 men, a 1983 comparison in 46 men and a 1991 high-dose placebo-controlled trial), a randomized comparison with testosterone undecanoate in 26 hypogonadal men, and a study in normal men of pituitary-testicular function.[7][8][9][10][11] A review of computer-analysed brain-wave profiles reported preliminary clinical antidepressant properties for mesterolone without extensive statistical results, and Wikipedia describes a small double-blind trial in depressed patients with symptom improvement and a Klinefelter study showing no change in plasma testosterone.[12][1] A 1980 study compared non-17-alpha-alkylated androgens, including mesterolone, with danazol and stanozolol in hereditary angioedema prophylaxis.[31] None assessed physique or appearance.

The user who documented a trial of Proviron alone reported stronger erections, better mood, a slightly drier look and slightly more vascularity, but no increase in muscle hardness, strength or mass and no effect on hair; he suggested it might help with sexual side effects from SSRIs, finasteride or deca.[3] A reply described it as very weak and mainly used alongside other steroids.[3] These are individual reports, not controlled data.
In published trials the measured outcomes were sexual activity, mood and semen parameters rather than muscle or appearance.[10][7][8]

Wikipedia lists virilization-type effects: acne, scalp hair loss, increased body hair, voice changes and increased libido.[1] Grokipedia lists virilization in women, prostatic effects, fluid retention and contraindication in pregnancy.[2] Published safety data specific to healthy users are scarce. Forum users ask whether short courses suppress the hormonal axis, and a thread about DHT-raising compounds and finasteride or topical minoxidil drew the reply that inhibiting 5-alpha-reductase does not act on an already-formed DHT derivative.[25][27] Doses above a threshold in a small depression trial significantly lowered luteinizing hormone and testosterone, according to Wikipedia.[1]

Wikipedia reports that mesterolone is sold under prescription in many countries, including the UK, Australia and South Africa, but has never been marketed in the US, Canada or New Zealand; it is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US, Schedule IV in Canada, S4 in Australia and Class C5 in Brazil.[1] Non-medical use is generally unlawful where it is controlled, and it is detected in doping control.[1][28]

Proviron is one of the more commonly mentioned adjunct compounds on looksmax.org; one thread asks why it is not discussed more, another is a megathread on benefits and side effects, and others ask where to source it.[5][32][33] Users pair it with other compounds in teen and adult plans, and the discussion of it as a puberty-maxxing compound comes up in threads from younger members.[34][35][4]

lore.intro: Proviron is discussed on looksmax.org as a mild, DHT-raising add-on, with some users calling it underrated and others calling it mostly ineffective.[4][3][5]

claims.claim: Proviron raises DHT and aids puberty-maxxing.
Proviron alone does little for muscle, hair or hardness.
It improves sperm count and fertility.
Raising DHT with Proviron will undo finasteride or increase hair loss.
It helps with sexual side effects of other drugs.
Its high SHBG binding raises free testosterone.
It is a gentle, liver-safe oral.
